message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This review is grounded in two months of actual till data for every main course, a full competitor price check, and the latest supplier information, so the recommendations are not guesswork. The price increases are modest and targeted: each of the three dishes stays below the midpoint of competitor prices for that dish, so we remain the value option in the area, and with 60% of bookings from repeat guests our customer base is loyal enough to absorb a pound or two. The projected effect is simple to check, £810 a week or about £42,000 a year in additional gross profit, which lifts our main-course margin to about 71%. I also think the menu-mix decision is clear-cut: the data show the mushroom risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so replacing it with a seasonal special is an easy improvement. Monitoring for eight weeks gives us an early warning if volumes move. Overall I believe these changes are sensible, low-risk and well evidenced.
</author>

<document>
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.
</document>
response:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

## Overall verdict

The price increases themselves are reasonable and correctly benchmarked. The case built around them doesn't hold up, though:

- **The risotto rationale is the opposite of what the data show.**
- **The profit projection ignores the beef cost increase that Section 4 itself reports.** Once that is included, the gain falls by about a third.
- **Once the beef increase and the risotto swap are included, main-course margin probably ends up no better than today**, not at 71%.

The author's summary describes the paper as "well evidenced." In practice, the evidence is collected but not used.

## Major issues

### 1. The risotto has the *strongest* margin on the menu, not the weakest

Table 1 gives the risotto an **80%** gross margin, the highest of any dish. In cash terms it earns **£11.20 per plate**. That's more than the burger (£10.80) or the curry (£10.90), and almost the same as fish and chips (£11.40).

| Dish | Gross profit per plate | Margin |
|---|---|---|
| Sirloin steak | £15.60 | 60% |
| Fish and chips | £11.40 | 69% |
| **Mushroom risotto** | **£11.20** | **80%** |
| Chicken curry | £10.90 | 75% |
| Beef burger | £10.80 | 72% |

The other half of the claim, "lowest sales," is also only a tie: the risotto sells 90 plates a week, the same as the specials.

Replacing it is likely to *reduce* profit. Specials currently run at a 64% margin. If the new vegetarian special matches that at £14, each plate earns about £2.24 less, which comes to **roughly £200 a week lost**. The risotto also appears to be the only vegetarian main on the fixed menu. One vegetarian diner can decide where a whole group books, so this change carries a risk the paper doesn't mention.

### 2. The projection ignores the beef increase

Section 4 says beef rises by 12% on 1 April, the same day the new prices start. Section 5.3 ignores it.

- Burger food cost: £4.20 to about £4.70, an extra £0.50 a plate, or about **£131 a week**.
- Steak food cost: £10.40 to about £11.65, an extra £1.25 a plate, or about **£150 a week**.

Together that's about **£281 a week** of extra cost. More than half of the extra £2 on the steak goes on the cost increase.

### 3. Corrected projection

| Scenario | Weekly | Annual (×52) |
|---|---|---|
| As stated in the paper | £810 | £42,120 |
| Less beef cost increase | ~£529 | ~£27,500 |
| Less risotto swap (special at 64% margin, £14) | ~£328 | ~£17,000 |

**If menu prices include VAT** (normal in the UK), the extra revenue is only five-sixths of the price rise: £675 a week, not £810. That cuts the figures further, to about £394 and £192 a week. The paper should state whether its prices and margins are net of VAT. If they aren't, every margin in Table 1 is overstated. Fish and chips, for example, would be about 63% rather than 69%.

### 4. The "about 71%" margin claim

Using the five dishes with known prices in Table 1:

- **Current** main-course margin: about **69.9%**.
- With the price increases only (the paper's case): about **71.3%**. The "about 71%" checks out on that basis.
- Adding the beef cost increase: about **69.7%**, roughly unchanged from today.
- Adding the risotto swap as well: about **68.5%**, *lower* than today.

Mains are already at roughly 70% on this basis. So the slide to 67% in overall food margin described in Section 1 may come from starters and desserts, not mains. The paper doesn't examine this.

## Other issues

**"Remain the value option."** Today these three dishes are the cheapest in the competitor group. After the increases, each will be *above* the cheapest competitor:
- fish and chips at £17.50 against £16.95
- burger at £16.00 against £15.50
- steak at £28.00 against £27.00

The prices will be below the midpoint, as claimed, but not the lowest.

**Day count.** Section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five days. The recommendation says "six trading days a week." The weekly figures don't depend on it, but one of the two statements is wrong.

**Competitor check.** It covers three dishes. The curry and the risotto weren't checked, so "full competitor price check" overstates it.

**Volumes.** "We expect volumes to hold" rests on loyalty and one earlier price change whose size isn't given. A useful addition would be the break-even volume loss. For example, fish and chips could lose about 8% of its volume before the higher price stopped paying for itself, and that's before the cost changes above.

**Monitoring.**
- The baseline is January–February, while the trial runs April–May, so seasonal change will be mixed up with any price effect. Comparing against April–May 2025 would be better.
- The plan tracks plates only. It should also track margin per dish, and covers by session, especially weekday lunch.
- The risk section calls lunch a "small share," but gives no figure. All the data show is that Friday and Saturday dinner is just under half of sales.

**Communication.** With 60% of bookings from repeat guests, regulars are the people most likely to notice a quiet increase. Not drawing attention to it may cost more goodwill than a short explanation that mentions the beef costs.

## Suggested changes before this goes to the owners

1. **Keep the risotto**, or justify its removal on grounds other than margin, such as kitchen time or waste. If it is replaced, state the target cost for the new dish.
2. **Restate the projection** to include the beef increase, give both VAT-inclusive and net figures, and show a downside case with, say, 5% lower volume.
3. **Consider raising the steak by more than £2.** Most of that £2 goes on beef costs, and £29 would still be below the £29.50 midpoint.
4. **Investigate starters and desserts** as the likely cause of the drop to 67%.
5. **Fix the day count**, and reword "value option" to "below the competitor midpoint."

The price increases look sensible. But on the paper's own data, the package as written delivers perhaps £17,000–£27,000 a year rather than £42,000, and it leaves main-course margin about where it is now.
